title: Demonstratives: οὗτος and ἐκεῖνος

objectives.can: Parse the forms of οὗτος and ἐκεῖνος and read them with a noun or alone.

explanation.summary: οὗτος means 'this' and ἐκεῖνος means 'that'. They point to a person or thing, and they agree with it in case, number and gender. Their forms are the article's with a few changes, and they are among the commonest words in the New Testament.

sections.heading: 'This' and 'that'
body: οὗτος points to what is near, or to what has just been mentioned. ἐκεῖνος points to what is further away, in space, time or the line of thought. These are the usual senses and not a rigid rule: context decides. The two words are classed as demonstrative pronouns, and the analysed texts mark them PronType=Dem even when they stand with a noun like an adjective.
Each has the three genders. οὗτος, αὕτη, τοῦτο are masculine, feminine and neuter singular; οὗτοι, αὗται, ταῦτα are the plurals. ἐκεῖνος, ἐκείνη, ἐκεῖνο are the three singular forms of 'that'.

sections.heading: The forms of οὗτος
body: The endings are those of the article: the genitive singular is τούτου and ταύτης, the dative plural τούτοις and ταύταις. The forms begin with τ-, except the four nominatives οὗτος, οὗτοι, αὕτη and αὗται, which, like the article, have a rough breathing instead.

What changes from one form to another is the vowel of the stem. Where the ending has an o-sound (masculine and neuter), the stem has ου: τούτου, τούτῳ, τούτων, τοῦτο. Where the ending has an α- or η-sound (feminine, and the neuter plural), the stem has αυ: ταύτην, ταύτης, ταῦτα. The neuter singular is τοῦτο, with no final -ν.

sections.heading: The forms of ἐκεῖνος
body: ἐκεῖνος is simpler. It has the ordinary endings of the second and first declensions: ἐκείνου, ἐκείνῳ, ἐκείνης, ἐκείνῃ, ἐκείνων. The neuter singular is ἐκεῖνο, with no -ν, like the article τό.

sections.heading: With a noun
body: When a demonstrative goes with a noun, the noun keeps its article, and the demonstrative stands outside it: either before the article, οὗτος ὁ ἄνθρωπος, or after the noun, ὁ ἄνθρωπος οὗτος. Both mean 'this man'. This is called the predicate position, and it differs from the adjective ἀγαθός, which can stand between the article and its noun. The demonstrative agrees with its noun in case, number and gender: ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ is dative singular feminine throughout, 'on that day'.
Greek keeps the article where English drops it: οὗτος ὁ ἄνθρωπος is 'this man', not 'this the man'.

sections.heading: Standing alone
body: Without a noun the demonstrative is a pronoun: 'this one', 'he', 'that one'. Its gender and number follow the person or thing it points to, and its case is the case it has in its own clause: Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱός μου, 'this is my son'. The neuter τοῦτο and ταῦτα often point to a fact, an event or a whole statement rather than to a single thing: 'this', 'these things'.

sections.heading: ὅδε and τοιοῦτος in brief
body: ὅδε, 'this here', is a stronger demonstrative that is rare in the New Testament. It appears in τάδε λέγει, 'thus says', which introduces a message, as in Acts 21:11, and in εἰς τήνδε τὴν πόλιν, 'into this city'. τοιοῦτος, 'such', has forms like those of οὗτος (τοιούτους, τοιαύτην) and is also counted as a demonstrative here.

misunderstandings: οὗτος is not οὕτως. The first is the pronoun 'this', the second is an adverb meaning 'in this way, so'. They differ in their last letters and in the accent.

αὕτη is not αὐτή. αὕτη has a rough breathing and means 'this' (feminine); αὐτή has a smooth breathing and is the feminine of αὐτός, 'she' or 'herself'. The breathing is the only sign, which is why it matters.
A demonstrative with a noun must agree with that noun, even when other words come between them. Alone, it takes its gender and number from what it points to and its case from its own clause.
The neuter τοῦτο is not always about one 'thing'. It often refers to a whole idea or to what has just been said.

deeper.heading: Why the forms look like the article
body: Grammarians explain οὗτος as the article with an added element, and that is why its endings are those of the article. The same added element is probably why the nominative forms keep the rough breathing. You do not need the history to read the forms, but it shows that the τ-/rough-breathing pattern of ὁ ἡ τό is the one to carry over.
